founder.whyTitle: Why me, and why in public
founder.whyParagraphs:
I can build the platform, run the experiment, and tell the story — those are three different skills and this project needs all three in one person at the start.

The important commitment is the honest part. The stipend is capped and time-boxed. My working hours are logged like every other metric. If running this experiment produces a worse life than the job it replaced, the experiment has failed and I will publish that.

summary.title: Pre-registered. Falsifiable. Published either way.
summary.intro: These commitments are published before any results exist, so the outcome cannot be reframed afterwards. This is what separates research from a diary.
summary.pillars:
Hypothesis | Removing financial survival pressure increases both the volume and the shipping rate of creative output.
Primary metric | Projects shipped per 90 days. Countable, objective, and hard to fudge.
Comparison group | 30 creators logging identical metrics without funding. Without this, a positive result cannot be interpreted.
Baseline | My own 90 days before funding, reconstructed from existing records — a limitation, stated in advance.
summary.quote: Kill criteria, stated in advance: if after 90 funded days shipped-projects-per-90-days shows no improvement over baseline and no separation from the comparison group, the hypothesis is published as failed — in full, with the raw data.

market.title: Three people pay for this. None of them are buying my rent.
market.intro: The experiment is the proof. The tool and the protocol are what people actually buy.
market.trends:
Financial scarcity demonstrably consumes cognitive bandwidth, producing risk-aversion and short-term thinking.
Funding people rather than ideas is a proven pattern: fellowships, residencies, and early accelerators all work this way.
Companies already pay for protected time — L&D budgets, innovation sprints, sabbatical benefits — but rarely measure what it produces.
market.opportunity: The gap is not a shortage of creative people. It is the absence of a repeatable, measurable way to buy them time.
market.competitiveIntro: Unlike accelerators that take equity, or residencies that select on prestige, this model:
market.advantages:
Sells no equity | No investment product, no revenue share, no returns. Subscriptions, gifts, and programme fees only.
Publishes its failures | Kill criteria are stated before the experiment begins and null results are published in full.
Is fully receipted | Every dollar in, every dollar out, every project to shipped or killed, in public.
Measures what it sells | The protocol exists because the measurement does. Sponsors buy the report, not the association.
market.audiences:
Creators | People who want to run the same experiment on themselves and want the protocol to do it.
Sponsors | Brands and foundations that already fund fellowships and want a novel piece of research attached.
Companies | Teams with L&D or innovation budgets looking for a structured innovation sabbatical with published outcomes.
Readers | People who simply want to watch a genuinely falsifiable experiment run in the open.

business.title: Three engines. In the order they earn.
business.intro: The story earns attention. The platform earns a little. The protocol, proven by the first two, earns the most.
business.pillars:
Audience | The experiment as serialised public content. Earns first, and makes everything else cheaper to sell.
Platform | Log, signal, track, and receipt ideas. Four modules, built only as the protocol needs them.
Protocol | The documented method, delivered to cohorts and licensed to companies. Earns last, and most.
Constraint | Stay small. A company whose thesis is that small is sufficient should not staff up to prove it.
business.platformTitle: A worked example of the protocol
business.platformIntro: The experiment generates the protocol. The protocol becomes a product a company can buy:
business.platformSteps:
A named cohort of 4–6 employees gets 8 weeks of protected time.
Every outcome is logged and measured against a baseline cohort.
The company receives an anonymised findings report it can point to internally.
business.platformClosing: Sold against an existing L&D or innovation budget line — not as a novelty.
business.revenueStreams:
Membership | $5–15/month for the log, the data, and a vote on which ideas get funded next. No equity, no returns.
Underwriting | $250 to fund one specific idea to completion, credited in the log.
Sponsored cohorts | ~$40,000 per cohort of 5 fellows on a ~$30,000 programme cost. The published report is what makes the price defensible.
B2B programmes | ~$20,000 per 8-week programme, four per year at maturity. Sold against existing training budgets.

financials.title: Start for under $500. Earn the right to raise.
financials.intro: Illustrative assumptions, not projections. Every figure is an input you can change — they exist to show the arithmetic.
financials.phases:
Stage 0 · Prove it free (weeks 1–6) | 30 days, publish daily, ship one small thing per week. Cost: under $500. Gate to the next stage: 30 published days and 200 people on a list.
Stage 1 · Membership (months 2–9) | 150 members at ~$9 = ~$1,350/mo. Funds the experiment, not the lifestyle. Gated on 100+ paying members.
Stage 2 · First cohort (months 9–18) | 5 fellows × $6,000 = $30,000 programme cost, sold at $40,000. Gross margin $10,000.
Stage 3 · B2B (month 18+) | Four 8-week programmes a year at ~$20,000. The company stops depending on one person's story.
financials.breakEvenNote: Illustrative combined revenue at maturity: ~$16k membership + ~$20k cohorts + ~$80k B2B, run by one operator plus contract help. Not a venture-scale outcome — deliberately. Ambition is better spent on depth than on a valuation story.
financials.fundingIntro: You need capital to quit, not to start. Stage 0 tests everything for less than a laptop:
financials.fundingUses:
A place to publish | Under $50. The experiment is the marketing, so this is the whole spend.
A mailing list | Free at this scale. Not a crowdfunding page — a list.
A comparison group | Ten creators is enough to start, thirty enough to publish. Recruited from readers.
A ledger habit | Costs nothing and establishes the single thing that differentiates the company.
financials.exitIntro: This model is designed to fail cheaply and publicly, which is the point:
financials.exitRoutes:
Stage 0 fails | Nobody reads and nothing ships. Learned for under $500, which is the cheapest and most valuable result available.
Hypothesis fails | The null result is published in full with raw data. The protocol itself survives and becomes the product.
No sponsor appears | Membership continues at a small scale. The experiment keeps running; the company does not scale.
Worst case | The experiment produces a worse life than the job did. Publish it, stop, and say so plainly.

ledger.title: Every dollar in. Every dollar out.
ledger.intro: The single most differentiating thing here. "Fund my life" is unaccountable by nature — so this is receipted, categorised, and public from day one.
ledger.moneyIn:
Patron subscriptions | $5–15/month. The base of the model; funds the experiment, never a salary above the cap.
Underwriting | $250 to carry one named idea to completion. Credited in the log, receipted in the ledger.
Sponsored cohorts | Single sponsor per cohort, priced against the published research report.
B2B programmes | Fixed programme fees. Sold under a plain descriptor, not the consumer brand.
ledger.moneyOut:
Living stipend (capped) | Capped and time-boxed by design. An experiment about sustainable output cannot run on the burnout it is meant to disprove.
Tools & services | Software, hosting, research instruments. Line-itemed, never lumped.
Platform costs | Domains, infrastructure, and contract development where needed.
Nothing else | No draws, no expenses without a category. If it is not on this list, it is not spent.
ledger.produced:
Projects shipped | The primary metric. Counted per 90 days and published whether the number is good or bad.
Ideas killed | Logged with the reason at the moment of killing, because abandonment reasons are the most interesting data here.
Data drops | Raw metrics released monthly, downloadable by anyone, including the comparison group's numbers.
Null results | Published in full. This is the commitment that makes the rest of it credible.
ledger.statNote: Starting balance. Publishing begins at zero, on purpose — the ledger is only worth anything if it is honest before there is anything in it.

modelsPage.title: Log. Signal. Track. Receipt.
modelsPage.intro: The protocol needs exactly four things to work. The platform builds those four and nothing else until they are used weekly. Every extra feature is a reason not to publish.
modelsPage.requirements: An 8-week innovation sabbatical for 4–6 employees. Protected time, a structured idea pipeline, all outcomes logged, and an anonymised findings report at the end.

features.title: Log
features.description: One daily entry: what was attempted, what shipped, what was killed, and how long it took. Public by default, private optional.

features.title: Signal
features.description: Readers vote on which ideas proceed. Attention becomes a funding signal instead of a vanity metric.

features.title: Track
features.description: Every idea carries to shipped or killed, with the reason logged at the moment of decision. No idea quietly disappears.

features.title: Ledger
features.description: Money in, money out, and what it produced — categorised and public. The accountability layer the whole model rests on.

privacyPage.title: What this is not.
privacyPage.intro: This page exists because the original version of this project asked for something it should not have. It offered potential equity on a public page, which invites securities regulation and is unfair to the people reading it.
privacyPage.body:
The current model sells subscriptions, gifts, and programme fees. It does not offer equity, revenue share, or financial returns of any kind, and it will not. Any future equity conversation happens with a lawyer and never appears on a public page.

The experiment also commits to publishing null results. If the hypothesis fails, it is published in full with the raw data. The protocol survives either way, because the protocol is the product.
